cards.title: Variables are labeled boxes
cards.body: A variable stores a value under a name so you can use it later: score = 0 creates a box called score holding 0. Python figures out the type by itself — no declarations needed.

cards.title: Know your four basic types
cards.body: int is a whole number (42), float has a decimal (3.14), str is text in quotes ("hello"), bool is True or False. Mixing them up causes most beginner errors, so learn to spot each one.
Stuck on what something is? type() tells you: type("7") says <class 'str'> — quotes make it text, not a number, even though it looks numeric.

name = "Zoe"
age = 20
is_student = True

A string, an integer, and a boolean, each in a labeled box. Later you can do print("Hi, " + name) and Python fills in Zoe.

cards.q: What is the type of "7" in Python?
cards.explain: Quotes always mean string in Python. "7" is text that happens to look like a number — 7 without quotes is the integer.

flashcards.back: A named box that stores a value for your code to use later.
Reports the type of a value, e.g. type(3.5) is float.
Quotes make it a string. Python sees text, not a numeric value.

choices: Stores 0 in a variable named score
questions.explain: A single = assigns. (Checking equality uses ==, with two signs.)

questions.q: Which of these is a float?
questions.explain: The decimal point makes it a float. 42 is an int, and quotes would make it a string.

choices: TypeError — can't add str and int
questions.explain: Python refuses to mix text and numbers with +. Convert first: int("10") + 5 gives 15.

questions.q: Which is a valid variable name?
questions.explain: Names use letters, digits, and underscores, and can't start with a digit. Hyphens are subtraction, not allowed.

questions.q: is_ready = False. What type is is_ready?
questions.explain: True and False (capital first letter) are booleans — Python's yes/no type.

cards.title: if makes decisions
cards.body: if score > 10: runs its block only when the condition is true. Add elif for more cases and else as the fallback. The colon and the indented block underneath are what make it Python.

cards.title: for repeats the work
cards.body: for i in range(5): runs the block five times with i taking 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. range(n) counts from 0 up to — but not including — n. Loops turn five lines of repetition into two.
Indentation is not style in Python — it is syntax. The indented block under if or for is the code that belongs to it. One stray space and the program means something else.

cards.q: How many times does for i in range(3): run its block?
cards.explain: range(3) produces 0, 1, 2 — three values, stopping before 3.

flashcards.back: Runs a block of code only when its condition is True.

flashcards.front: Why does indentation matter in Python?
flashcards.back: It defines which lines belong to an if/for block — it is syntax, not decoration.

flashcards.front: What does a while loop do?
flashcards.back: Repeats its block as long as its condition stays True.

questions.q: x = 7. Which branch runs? if x > 10: ... elif x > 5: ... else: ...
questions.explain: 7 is not > 10, so the if fails; 7 is > 5, so the elif catches it. Python takes the first true branch.

questions.q: What prints? for c in "ab": print(c)
choices: a then b, on separate lines
questions.explain: Strings are sequences, so for walks each character: a, then b.

questions.q: Fix the bug: if temperature > 30 print("hot")
questions.explain: Every if needs a colon before its indented block. Without it, Python throws a syntax error.

questions.q: How do you loop exactly 10 times?
questions.explain: range(10) gives 0-9: exactly ten values. range(1, 10) gives only nine.

questions.q: while True: with no break inside does what?
questions.explain: True never becomes False, so the loop never exits. Always give a while loop a way out.

cards.title: def packages the work
cards.body: def greet(): defines a reusable block; greet() runs it. Writing the def just stores the recipe — nothing happens until you call it with the parentheses.

cards.title: Inputs in, outputs out
cards.body: Parameters are the inputs a function expects: def add(a, b):. return hands a value back to the caller and stops the function immediately. No return? The caller gets None.
Name functions like actions: calculate_total, send_email, is_valid. If you can't name it as a verb, you probably don't know what it does yet.

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(2, 3)  # result is 5

Define once, call anywhere. add(10, 20) works just as well — the function doesn't care which numbers you hand it.

cards.q: What does a function with no return statement give back?
cards.explain: Falling off the end of a function quietly returns None — Python's 'nothing here' value.

flashcards.front: How do you define and call a function?
flashcards.back: def name(): to define, name() to call.
Parameter is the name in the definition (a, b); argument is the value passed at call time (2, 3).
Sends a value back to the caller and exits the function immediately.
Python's 'no value' — what a function returns when it has no return statement.

questions.q: What does greet() do if greet was defined with def greet():?
questions.explain: The parentheses are the go button. def only defines; calling executes.

questions.q: def double(n): return n * 2 — what is double(4)?
questions.explain: n becomes 4, 4 * 2 is 8, and return hands 8 back.

choices: Function names can't start with a digit
questions.explain: Names follow the same rules as variables: letters, digits, underscores, never starting with a digit.

questions.q: Inside a function: x = 1; x = x + 1; return x. Result?
questions.explain: x starts at 1, becomes 2, and return sends 2 back. Assignment updates the box.

questions.q: When should you write a function?
choices: When you need the same logic in more than one place
For every single line of code
questions.explain: Functions exist to kill repetition. Two or more uses of the same steps is the signal to package them.
